extracted.intended_audience: Reviewers (and prospective reviewers) for the Journal of Open Source Software (JOSS)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for conducting peer review of JOSS submissions, focusing on software quality, development practices, and required paper content, plus procedural expectations (timing, COI, issue tracking).

rubrics_metrics.name: Software best practices (documentation, tests, CI, license)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the submitting authors have followed best practices (have documentation, tests, continuous integration, and a license) then their review should be rapid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JOSS is 'developer friendly' and expects these elements; lack thereof is a reason to give clear feedback on how to improve. Treat presence of documentation, tests, CI, and an explicit license as positive indicators of readiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check against the JOSS review checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: A JOSS review involves checking submissions against a checklist covering software quality, development practices, and required paper content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviews should be objective and based on the materials in the submission. Use the checklist items to make concrete, verifiable assessments rather than subjective impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clear constructive feedback for improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: For submissions that don’t quite meet the bar, please try to give clear feedback on how authors could improve their submission. A key goal of JOSS is to raise the quality of research software generally and you (the experienced reviewer) are well placed to give this feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific about what needs changing and how; point to actionable steps and examples rather than vague criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time expectations for reviewers (timeliness)
rubrics_metrics.description: We ask reviewers to complete their reviews in 4-6 weeks. We aim for the first pass of reviews to be completed within about 2-4 weeks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you require more time, let the editor know up front. Use EditorialBot to set automatic reminders if you'll be away. Being clear about availability helps editors work with authors and keep papers moving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors' expected response timings
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should respond to your feedback within 2 weeks and complete requested changes within 4-6 weeks, unless otherwise negotiated with the editor (for example, if the changes requested are particularly substantial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If authors are unresponsive, the editor will follow up. Reviewers should be aware of these norms when assessing progress and setting expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity and impartial assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: This should be objective, not subjective; it should be based on the materials in the submission as perceived without distortion by personal feelings, prejudices, or interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on evidence in the submission. Avoid letting personal tastes or unrelated disputes influence your evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: File issues on the submitted repository's issue tracker
rubrics_metrics.description: We encourage reviewers to file issues against the submitted repository’s issue tracker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can include in your review links to any new issues that you the reviewer believe to be impeding the acceptance of the repository. If the submitted repository is a GitHub repository, mentioning the review issue URL in the submitted repository’s issue tracker will create a mention in the review issue’s history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record completion in the review issue
rubrics_metrics.description: When you have completed your review, please leave a comment in the review issue saying so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the review issue as the authoritative record of review progress; include links to repository issues that block acceptance if relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest (COI) disclosure and rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of a conflict of Interest in peer review is a circumstance that makes you 'unable to make an impartial scientific judgment or evaluation.' JOSS is concerned with avoiding any actual conflicts of interest, and being sufficiently transparent that we avoid the appearance of conflicts of interest as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a reviewer (or editor), COIs include: recent (past four years) collaborators in funded research or published work; lifetime for family members, business partners, and thesis student/advisor or mentor; and recent (past year) association with the same organization of a submitter (e.g., being employed at the same institution). If you have a COI, disclose the specific reason to the submission's editor. Some conflicts may be recorded and waived; if you think you can make an impartial assessment you may request a waiver. If in doubt, ask the editors. The page gives examples of waivable situations (e.g., being one of 2000 authors on a paper, or a collaboration published 6 years ago but appearing recently due to delays).

rubrics_metrics.name: When authors are unresponsive
rubrics_metrics.description: If an author becomes unresponsive, the editor will follow up to keep the review moving forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should notify editors if they have availability issues; editors will handle follow-up if authors do not respond in the expected windows.
